synopsis: Chapter 12 and the glossary cite Buehler, Griffin and Ross’s 1994 research as evidence of systematic underestimation of completion times for academic and non-academic tasks [f9598, f16312]. Only 29.7% of students finished their thesis by their own best-estimate date [f9599, f16311]. Underestimation persisted even when participants were instructed to be pessimistic, and participants focused on their current plan rather than relevant past outcomes [f9600, f9601, f16312]. The glossary rates the planning-fallacy finding as proven; the supplied facts agree across locations but provide no quantified application to this booklet’s validation-project schedule [f16312, f9598, f9599, f9600, f9601, f16311].

relations.note: Both report 29.7% thesis completion by students’ own best-estimate dates.
Both report persistent underestimation despite pessimistic instructions.
Both report focus on current plans rather than relevant past outcomes.
Low on-time thesis completion supports the broader finding of underestimated completion times.
Adds persistence under pessimistic instructions, plan-focused thinking, and the booklet’s proven rating.
Thesis completion statistic provides quantitative evidence for the planning-fallacy finding.
